web_title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Stock Cycles
book_title: From Manhattan Apothecary to America's Healthcare Toll Road
question: How did a 19th-century New York drug importer survive two historic accounting scandals, hostile takeovers, and an $8 billion opioid reckoning to become the largest pharmaceutical logistics engine in North America?

epigraph.quote: Distribution is the unglamorous plumbing of capitalism—until the pipes clog, and everyone discovers who actually owns the infrastructure.
epigraph.author: Institutional Supply Chain Maxim

web_blocks.title: 1833–1938: The Manhattan Importer, National Roll-Up, and the Coster Scandal

web_blocks.html: McKesson Corporation's roots stretch back nearly two centuries to 1833. John McKesson and Charles Olcott opened Olcott & McKesson on Maiden Lane in New York City [16, 17]. Their model was simple: import botanical drugs, therapeutic chemicals, and apothecary goods from Europe, then sell them to local druggists across the United States [16, 17]. After Olcott died in 1853, longtime employee Daniel Robbins became a partner, creating McKesson & Robbins [16, 17]. Two years later, in 1855, the firm entered drug manufacturing. It made fluid extracts, tinctures, pills, and tablets that won global acclaim [16, 17].

By the early 1900s, U.S. drug distribution remained split across hundreds of local jobbers. In the 1920s, McKesson & Robbins launched a sweeping roll-up, persuading regional wholesalers to join as subsidiaries [16, 17]. From 1928 to 1937, the firm bought wholesale drug houses in 47 U.S. and Canadian cities [17]. Sales hit $140 million by 1929, creating the nation's first coast-to-coast drug network [17].

That rapid growth set the stage for McKesson's first crisis in 1938. CEO F. Donald Coster was later unmasked as Philip Musica, a twice-convicted fraudster using an alias [16, 17]. A skeptical treasurer spotted cash-flow gaps in the crude-drug unit [16, 17]. Probes showed that roughly $19 million—one-quarter of the $86.6 million in reported assets—was fake inventory and phantom Canadian warehouses [16, 17]. The scandal reshaped U.S. corporate rules. It pushed the SEC and accounting bodies to require physical inventory checks and direct receivables confirmation [16]. Even so, McKesson's wholesale routes were vital to U.S. pharmacies. The firm survived receivership in the early 1940s with its core distribution network intact [16, 17].

web_blocks.title: 1967–2017: Conglomerate Detours, the HBOC Collapse, and Specialty Seeds

web_blocks.html: In 1967, San Francisco-based Foremost Dairies took over McKesson & Robbins in a hostile bid. That formed Foremost-McKesson Inc., an unfocused group spanning dairy, liquor, chemicals, real estate, and drug wholesaling [16, 17]. After fending off a 1976 raid by Victor Posner, management spent years selling side businesses [17]. In 1982–1983, the firm sold its Foremost dairy unit and adopted the name McKesson Corporation [16, 17]. It then committed to pure-play healthcare distribution [16, 17].

In the early 1990s, McKesson built PCS Health Systems, an early pharmacy benefit manager (PBM). After Merck bought Medco for $6.6 billion in 1993, McKesson sold PCS to Eli Lilly for $4 billion in cash in 1994 [17]. It paid $76 per share to owners and invested $600 million in warehouse automation [17]. Five years later, management hit its second major accounting crisis. In 1999, McKesson bought healthcare IT firm HBO & Company (HBOC) to form McKessonHBOC [16]. Within months, auditors found widespread premature revenue-recognition fraud at HBOC, leading to prosecutions and a governance overhaul [16].

Over the next fifteen years, McKesson rebuilt trust by focusing on operations and adding high-margin adjacencies. It bought US Oncology in 2010 to anchor community cancer care and grew in Canada and Europe [16]. In 2017, it bought CoverMyMeds, a key software deal that later anchored Prescription Technology Solutions (RxTS) [16].

web_blocks.title: 2018–2026: Opioid Reckoning, European Exit, and the Specialty Pivot

web_blocks.html: From 2016 to 2022, McKesson and its Big Three peers faced their worst legal threat: thousands of opioid lawsuits. McKesson had paid $13.25 million in 2008 and $300 million in 2017 for Controlled Substances Act reporting failures [16, 21]. Industry-wide trial exposure was estimated up to $95 billion [16, 21]. In FY2021, McKesson booked huge litigation charges that drove a $5.04 billion GAAP operating loss [15]. In 2022, McKesson, Cencora, and Cardinal Health reached a $21 billion national settlement over 18 years [16, 21]. McKesson's share was capped at $7.9 billion, turning an open-ended threat into a predictable annual cash payment [16, 21].

At the same time, McKesson moved its headquarters from San Francisco to Irving, Texas in April 2019. That move coincided with Brian Tyler becoming CEO [16]. Tyler also became Board Chair on May 1, 2026, and Kenny Cheung became CFO on May 29, 2026 [1, 5]. Under their lead, McKesson executed a three-part shift. First, it exited lower-margin European retail and distribution, closing the final Norway sale on January 30, 2026 [11]. Second, it exited Change Healthcare in 2020 and invested in oncology and specialty MSOs [5, 13]. It bought controlling stakes in Florida Cancer Specialists' Core Ventures, PRISM Vision Holdings, and Precision Medicine Group ($2.25 billion, closed November 2, 2026) [5, 8, 13, 14]. It also signed a $1.4 billion deal for a 49% stake in Option Care Health [5, 12]. Third, in FY2026–FY2027 it moved to spin off Medical-Surgical Solutions as Wellverse, selling a 13% stake to Apollo Funds for $1.25 billion in June 2026 [9].

web_blocks.takeaway: Across nearly two centuries, McKesson survived every crisis—from 1938 inventory fraud to 2022 opioid settlements—because its physical drug-delivery toll road remained indispensable to U.S. pharmacies and hospitals.

web_blocks.mechanism: A mid-tier medical-surgical distributor lost scale in hospital supply and suffered contract churn. It then tried to pivot into capital-heavy PPE manufacturing (Halyard Health) using debt-funded M&A at peak pandemic demand.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: It spent ~$710M for Halyard Health (2018) and ~$1.6B for Apria (2022). Post-pandemic PPE deflation then crushed margins, pushing net leverage to ~4x–5x EBITDA and triggering a >70% stock drop from ~$49 in 2021 to below $15 by 2024–2025.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Sub-scale middlemen without specialty networks or software lock-in get squeezed from both ends. McKesson's move to separate Medical-Surgical (Wellverse) while doubling down on Oncology and RxTS avoids the Owens & Minor trap.

web_blocks.title: Past Business Cycles: Why Wholesale Volume Endures While Margins Breathe
paragraphs: Unlike cyclical industrials, McKesson's prescription volumes grew through recessions, pandemics, and rate shocks because chronic drugs are non-discretionary [18].

Instead, McKesson's past earnings cycles stemmed from three internal and policy forces. First, generic drug price deflation hit from 2016 to 2018 [19]. Second, major contract shifts moved volume, such as winning UnitedHealth's $35B+ OptumRx contract from Cardinal Health in mid-2025 while absorbing Rite Aid's bankruptcy [9, 19]. Third, one-time legal charges hit GAAP results, led by the FY2021 opioid accrual [15].

web_blocks.html: The pattern across two centuries is clear. Accounting scandals and conglomerate detours hurt shareholders temporarily, yet they never broke the core delivery routes. Whenever management returned to disciplined capital allocation, cash flow recovered quickly. Today's North American focus leaves McKesson leaner and far more profitable per dollar of invested capital [2, 11].

book_paragraphs: To understand McKesson Corporation, start with a paradox. Here is a firm founded in 1833 on Manhattan's Maiden Lane that moves over $400 billion of medicine a year [1, 16, 17]. Yet most Americans have never seen a McKesson storefront. You do not walk into a McKesson pharmacy. You walk into CVS, a community cancer clinic, or a hospital infusion center. McKesson is the invisible circulatory system that put the vial on the shelf hours earlier.

Before trusting any 193-year-old firm, ask a hard question: how did it survive crises that kill normal companies? McKesson did not just survive. It endured two infamous accounting scandals, a hostile takeover, and an opioid reckoning—and came out stronger.

Picture 1938. The firm, then McKesson & Robbins, was led by a suave executive named F. Donald Coster [17]. Nobody knew Coster was actually Philip Musica, a twice-convicted fraudster who had even landed in Who's Who in America [17]. For over a decade, Coster rolled up regional drug wholesalers across 47 cities, building the first national footprint [17]. Then a sharp treasurer asked why a booming crude-drug unit never seemed to produce real cash [17]. Investigators found that roughly $19 million—a quarter of the $86.6 million in reported assets—did not exist [16, 17]. The fraud forced the SEC and accountants to invent modern physical inventory audits [16]. Yet the wholesale routes were so vital to U.S. druggists that McKesson reorganized and kept delivering [16, 17].

In 1967, Foremost Dairies launched a hostile takeover, turning McKesson into a bloated dairy, liquor, and real-estate group [16, 17]. Management spent fifteen years fighting raiders like Victor Posner and selling side units. It finally sold the dairy business in 1982–1983 to become pure-play McKesson Corporation [16, 17]. In 1994, management sold its early PBM unit, PCS Health Systems, to Eli Lilly for $4 billion [17]. It returned $76 per share to owners and put $600 million into warehouse automation [17]. That automation investment laid the groundwork for modern high-speed distribution.

Five years later, in 1999, McKesson made a classic empire-building mistake. It bought healthcare software firm HBO & Company at the height of the dot-com boom [16]. Within months, HBOC's books unraveled in a huge revenue-recognition scandal [16]. Once again, critics wrote McKesson off. Once again, the core logistics engine kept churning out cash while management fixed governance, bought US Oncology in 2010, and bought CoverMyMeds in 2017 [16]. Those two deals planted the seeds for McKesson's highest-margin growth engines today.

Then came the existential test of our own era: the opioid crisis. From 2008 to 2017, McKesson paid hundreds of millions in federal fines for failing to flag suspicious orders [16, 21]. By 2021, thousands of lawsuits threatened to bankrupt the wholesale industry, with claims up to $95 billion [16]. McKesson booked a $5.04 billion GAAP operating loss in FY2021 to accrue its share of a 2022 national settlement [15, 21]. Its cap of up to $7.9 billion over 18 years did something vital for owners. It turned an open-ended threat into a known, bond-like annual cash outflow [16, 21]. Investors could finally model the business again without fearing sudden legal ruin.

Since Brian Tyler became CEO in April 2019 and moved headquarters to Irving, Texas, McKesson has executed a clean transformation [1, 16]. Look at the receipts. First, Tyler exited low-margin European retail and distribution, closing the final Norway sale in January 2026 [11]. Second, he leaned hard into community oncology. McKesson bought controlling stakes in Core Ventures and PRISM Vision, closed the $2.25 billion Precision Medicine Group deal in November 2026, and signed a $1.4 billion deal for 49% of Option Care Health [5, 8, 12, 14]. Third, in 2026, management began spinning off Medical-Surgical as Wellverse, bringing in Apollo Funds for a $1.25 billion minority stake [9].

Think about the Owens & Minor cautionary tale here. When mid-tier medical distributors lose scale or chase capital-heavy manufacturing at the wrong time, margins vanish. McKesson saw that Medical-Surgical had different capital needs than specialty oncology and biopharma software. Instead of letting it dilute the core engine, management carved it out to stand alone [9]. What remains is a sharper, faster, higher-margin North American healthcare toll road. Over nearly two centuries, every crisis has tested the moat, and every time the moat has held.

Remember that historical lesson as we move into the operating segments in Chapter 2. McKesson survived 1938, 1999, and 2021 because pharmacies and cancer clinics cannot function without its daily deliveries [16, 17]. Management's job is to protect that physical network while shifting capital into higher-margin specialty services and software [2, 9]. That balance between stability and growth is rare in modern healthcare.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: History does not repeat verbatim, but institutional DNA persists. McKesson's 193-year survival proves its physical network is a quasi-utility. Still, its 1938, 1999, and 2021 crises remind us that governance lapses and M&A missteps are the only forces capable of derailing it.
